findings: The frozen repository context contains two equivalent RocketMQ consumption-mode source wordings and no extra requirement that would justify broadening the Canonical into a general consumer-API survey. The candidate answers the common interview meaning immediately: Clustering and Broadcasting.

Apache RocketMQ 4.x official consumer documentation explicitly states that RocketMQ has two consumption modes, Clustering and Broadcasting. It supports the candidate's core distinction that same-group consumers share messages in Clustering while each same-group consumer receives the full message stream in Broadcasting.

The candidate correctly makes Consumer Group the comparison boundary. This prevents the common overstatement that a clustered message is consumed only once globally; different Consumer Groups can subscribe independently while the clustering/broadcasting distinction governs delivery inside the group.

The classification boundary is unusually important for this question and is handled well. Official RocketMQ documentation separately discusses Push/Pull and current PushConsumer/SimpleConsumer/PullConsumer consumer types, while the 4.x PushConsumer page separately distinguishes concurrent and orderly consumption. The answer therefore does not inflate the classic two MessageModel modes into four or more modes.

The 4.x API/version claim is scoped correctly: the candidate says the 4.x Java PushConsumer documentation exposes MessageModel.CLUSTERING/BROADCASTING and uses clustering by default, rather than asserting that this exact API surface is universal across all RocketMQ versions and client models.

The mechanism section explains why cluster mode needs load balancing/rebalancing and why adding a broadcast consumer duplicates full-stream processing rather than dividing one workload. The scaling boundary is stated with appropriate limits instead of promising linear throughput.

The project section does not fabricate production traffic, lag numbers, retries or company usage. It provides a decision mapping from delivery semantics to MessageModel and then to consumer type, concurrency/order, retry and idempotency. The three-minute section is longer than literal oral timing, so oral quality is scored 4/5.
